fields.topic_name: Probability foundations: events, conditional probability and information timing
fields.description:
Probability & Statistics · Week 1 · Day 1: Probability foundations: events, conditional probability and information timing

Study type: Probability/statistics + Python research. Duration: 150 minutes (2h 30m). Goal: Recover the probability rules needed to reason about uncertain outcomes, and express them using the timestamp at which a market forecast would actually be made. The mathematical material below is an explicit supplemental prerequisite refresher; Géron is still the primary ML book.

Reading and code references

  • ProbabilityCourse: Introduction to Probability, Statistics and Random Processes; review the relevant events, conditional probability, random variables or limit-theorem sections.
  • OpenIntro Statistics: free statistics textbook; read the appropriate probability, distributions, sampling or inference sections.
  • Géron Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape — official chapter notebook. Read the relevant chapter section; run the notebook only after checking the dataset and prediction-time assumptions.

Four detailed subtopics

1. Events and sample spaces

Define a sample space, events, complements and intersections. Explain why the event “tomorrow’s return exceeds zero” is measurable only after tomorrow closes, while today’s available features belong to the information set at the forecast timestamp.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

2. Axioms and addition rule

Use nonnegativity, normalization and additivity to derive the inclusion–exclusion rule. For two partly overlapping risk events, compute P(A union B) correctly instead of summing overlapping probabilities twice.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

3. Conditional probability

Write P(A given B) as P(A intersection B) divided by P(B), provided P(B) is positive. Compare unconditional and conditional probabilities for a market event during high-volatility and ordinary regimes.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

4. Independence and financial dependence

Distinguish statistical independence from zero linear correlation. Explain why time-adjacent returns or overlapping prediction labels violate common independent-sample assumptions, affecting effective sample size and validation.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

Independent Python experiment

Create probability_foundations.ipynb. Simulate events A and B from categorical outcomes; calculate marginal, joint and conditional probabilities analytically and by Monte Carlo; add a toy market-regime column and a forecast timestamp.

Time budget (adjust within 2–3 hours as needed)

  • Read theory, derive formulas and take short notes: 45 minutes
  • Work textbook or online exercises / run reference notebook: 30 minutes
  • Implement and rerun independent Python experiments: 60 minutes
  • Write findings, tests and limitations: 15 minutes

Definition of done

Notebook includes event definitions, a 2×2 contingency table, four calculated probabilities, independent-versus-dependent simulations, and three unit tests.

Research integrity: Record all random seeds, assumptions and sample definitions. Do not allow information published after the prediction timestamp into features. Make confidence and significance claims only under stated assumptions and report null results alongside positive ones.

fields.topic_name: Bayes theorem, base rates and posterior predictive thinking
fields.description:
Probability & Statistics · Week 1 · Day 2: Bayes theorem, base rates and posterior predictive thinking

Study type: Probability/statistics + Python research. Duration: 165 minutes (2h 45m). Goal: Turn classifier outputs and rare-event alarms into well-calibrated probabilities rather than confusing a strong signal with a high posterior event probability. The mathematical material below is an explicit supplemental prerequisite refresher; Géron is still the primary ML book.

Reading and code references

  • ProbabilityCourse: Introduction to Probability, Statistics and Random Processes; review the relevant events, conditional probability, random variables or limit-theorem sections.
  • OpenIntro Statistics: free statistics textbook; read the appropriate probability, distributions, sampling or inference sections.
  • Géron Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape — official chapter notebook. Read the relevant chapter section; run the notebook only after checking the dataset and prediction-time assumptions.
  • Géron Chapter 3: Classification — official chapter notebook. Read the relevant chapter section; run the notebook only after checking the dataset and prediction-time assumptions.

Four detailed subtopics

1. Prior, likelihood and evidence

Identify the prior probability of an event, likelihood of a signal given the event, and marginal chance of the signal. Derive the total-probability denominator so a posterior is a normalized probability.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

2. Bayes theorem and base-rate neglect

Compute P(crash given alarm) from P(alarm given crash), specificity and the low crash base rate. Even an apparently accurate alarm may yield a modest positive predictive value when the underlying event is rare.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

3. Posterior odds and likelihood ratios

Express posterior odds as prior odds times the likelihood ratio. Use this identity to reason about sequential evidence, while identifying when correlated evidence cannot be multiplied as if independent.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

4. Calibration versus discrimination

Separate ranking ability from probabilistic accuracy. Outline a reliability diagram and Brier score; observe that a classifier with high ROC-AUC can still report unreliable 0.9 probabilities.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

Independent Python experiment

Implement a rare-market-event alarm with fixed sensitivity and false-positive rate. Compute posterior probabilities by hand, Python formulas and simulation; sweep the base rate and plot positive predictive value.

Time budget (adjust within 2–3 hours as needed)

  • Read theory, derive formulas and take short notes: 49 minutes
  • Work textbook or online exercises / run reference notebook: 33 minutes
  • Implement and rerun independent Python experiments: 66 minutes
  • Write findings, tests and limitations: 17 minutes

Definition of done

Three independent posterior calculations agree within Monte Carlo error, plots show the base-rate effect, and a short note explains a realistic failure mode.

Research integrity: Record all random seeds, assumptions and sample definitions. Do not allow information published after the prediction timestamp into features. Make confidence and significance claims only under stated assumptions and report null results alongside positive ones.

Probability & Statistics · Week 1 · Day 3: Random variables and distributions: Bernoulli to heavy tails

Study type: Probability/statistics + Python research. Duration: 180 minutes (3h 0m). Goal: Choose probability distributions that match the measurement process instead of automatically assuming all financial observations are normal. The mathematical material below is an explicit supplemental prerequisite refresher; Géron is still the primary ML book.

Reading and code references

  • ProbabilityCourse: Introduction to Probability, Statistics and Random Processes; review the relevant events, conditional probability, random variables or limit-theorem sections.

  • Géron Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project — official chapter notebook. Read the relevant chapter section; run the notebook only after checking the dataset and prediction-time assumptions.

Four detailed subtopics

1. PMF, PDF and CDF

Define discrete mass functions, continuous densities and cumulative distribution functions. The probability of a continuous variable equaling an exact value is zero; calculate interval probabilities using CDF differences.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

2. Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson

Recognize Bernoulli outcomes for correct/incorrect forecast indicators, binomial counts under independent trials, and Poisson models for event arrivals. State the assumptions and why clustered financial events often violate Poisson independence.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

3. Normal and Student-t distributions

Compare center, dispersion and tail thickness. Student-t with low degrees of freedom produces more outliers than a normal distribution; use survival probabilities to quantify extreme observations rather than inferring safety from variance alone.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

4. Lognormal and empirical returns

Explain why prices are positive while arithmetic and log returns may be negative. Plot empirical quantiles, QQ plots and tail counts; distinguish descriptive distribution fits from a justified predictive model.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

Independent Python experiment

Use scipy.stats to simulate five named distributions. Estimate 1% tail thresholds, compare normal and Student-t exceedance counts on synthetic return data, and create QQ and histogram diagnostics.

  • Implement and rerun independent Python experiments: 72 minutes
  • Write findings, tests and limitations: 18 minutes

Probability & Statistics · Week 1 · Day 4: Expectation, variance, covariance and portfolio dependence

Study type: Probability/statistics + Python research. Duration: 165 minutes (2h 45m). Goal: Connect statistical moments to forecast loss, portfolio variance, model uncertainty and the limitations of simple correlation. Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

Calculate joint covariation and standardized Pearson correlation. Zero correlation does not imply independence; compare a nonlinear paired sample where dependence exists despite near-zero correlation.

4. Portfolio risk and covariance matrices

Build a covariance matrix and calculate two-asset variance using weights and cross-covariance. Examine positive semidefiniteness, unstable estimates, short windows and why diversifying by asset label alone is insufficient.

fields.description:
Probability & Statistics · Week 2 · Day 1: Sampling design, selection bias, missing data and estimands

Study type: Probability/statistics + Python research. Duration: 150 minutes (2h 30m). Goal: Learn what population a statistical claim concerns and how market-data selection can distort estimates before any model is trained. The mathematical material below is an explicit supplemental prerequisite refresher; Géron is still the primary ML book.

Reading and code references

  • OpenIntro Statistics: free statistics textbook; read the appropriate probability, distributions, sampling or inference sections.
  • Géron Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project — official chapter notebook. Read the relevant chapter section; run the notebook only after checking the dataset and prediction-time assumptions.

Four detailed subtopics

1. Population, sample and estimand

Separate the population of interest, data actually observed and statistic to estimate. A research question about all stocks cannot be answered unbiasedly by examining only currently listed survivors.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

2. Random sampling and time sampling

Compare independent random samples with chronological time-series observations. Price bars share market conditions, overlapping labels and common shocks, making naive sample-count interpretations optimistic.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

3. Survivorship and selection bias

Create a simulated universe in which weak firms exit. Compare a strategy’s measured returns with and without delisted members; document why removing failures creates a structurally optimistic sample.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

4. Missingness and data cleaning

Distinguish missing completely at random, missing at random and missing not at random. Explain why forward-filling released macro data or prices across inappropriate gaps can introduce misleading histories.

Explore: reference, formulas and documentation. Make a worked mathematical example and verify it with a Python calculation or simulation.

Independent Python experiment

Generate a panel of 100 simulated securities with entry and delisting dates. Compare a mean-return estimator for the full investable universe and a survivors-only panel; log missingness and leakage rules.

Time budget (adjust within 2–3 hours as needed)

  • Read theory, derive formulas and take short notes: 45 minutes
  • Work textbook or online exercises / run reference notebook: 30 minutes
  • Implement and rerun independent Python experiments: 60 minutes
  • Write findings, tests and limitations: 15 minutes
